statement: Of the various methods suggested for bleaching palm oil, the bichromate process originated by Watts is undoubtedly the best.
source_passage: Of the various methods suggested for bleaching palm oil, the bichromate process originated by Watts is undoubtedly the best.

statement: In the bichromate process for bleaching palm oil, potassium bichromate reacts with fourteen molecules of hydrochloric acid to give two of potassium chloride, one of chromic chloride, seven of water and six atoms of chlorine.
source_passage: The reaction may be expressed by the following equation, though in practice it is necessary to use twice the amount of acid required by theory:-- K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7} + 14HCl = 2KCl + Cr_{2}Cl_{6} + 7H_{2}O + 6Cl.

statement: In the bichromate process for bleaching palm oil, the six atoms of chlorine liberated react with three molecules of water to give six molecules of hydrochloric acid and three atoms of oxygen.
source_passage: 6Cl + 3H_{2}O = 6HCl + 3O.

statement: In practice, the bichromate process for bleaching palm oil requires twice the amount of acid required by theory.
source_passage: The reaction may be expressed by the following equation, though in practice it is necessary to use twice the amount of acid required by theory:--

statement: In the bichromate bleaching of palm oil, the palm oil is first freed from solid impurities by melting and subsidence, then placed in the bleaching tank and washed with water containing a little hydrochloric acid.
source_passage: The palm oil, freed from solid impurities by melting and subsidence, is placed in the bleaching tank, and washed with water containing a little hydrochloric acid.

statement: In the bichromate bleaching of palm oil, after the acid wash the oil is allowed to rest and the liquor and sediment (chiefly sand) are drawn off, after which the oil is ready for treatment with the bleaching reagent of potassium bichromate and commercial muriatic acid.
source_passage: Having allowed it to rest, and drawn off the liquor and sediment (chiefly sand), the palm oil is ready for treatment with the bleaching reagent, which consists of potassium bichromate and commercial muriatic acid.

statement: In the bichromate bleaching of palm oil, 22 to 28 lb. potassium bichromate and 45 to 60 lb. acid for every ton of oil will be found sufficient to produce a good bleached oil.
source_passage: For every ton of oil, 22 to 28 lb. potassium bichromate and 45 to 60 lb. acid will be found sufficient to produce a good bleached oil.

statement: The best procedure in the bichromate bleaching of palm oil is to act upon the colouring matter three successive times, using one-third of the average quantities of bichromate and acid in each of the first two treatments, and in the final treatment a quantity gauged by the appearance of a cooled sample of the oil.
source_passage: The best procedure is to act upon the colouring matter of the oil three successive times, using in the first two treatments one-third of the average of the figures just given, and in the final treatment an appropriate quantity which can be easily gauged by the appearance of a cooled sample of the oil.

statement: In the bichromate bleaching of palm oil, the potassium bichromate is dissolved in hot water and added to the crude palm oil previously heated to 125 deg. F. (52 deg. C.), then the muriatic acid is run in and the whole well agitated by means of air.
source_passage: The potassium bichromate is dissolved in hot water and added to the crude palm oil, previously heated to 125 deg. F. (52 deg. C.), the requisite amount of muriatic acid being then run in and the whole well agitated by means of air.

statement: During the bichromate bleaching of palm oil, the bright red colour of the oil gradually changes to dark brown and soon becomes green.
source_passage: The bright red colour of the oil gradually changes to dark brown, and soon becomes green.

statement: In the bichromate bleaching of palm oil, after the action has proceeded for a few minutes, agitation is stopped, the mixture is allowed to settle, and the green liquor is withdrawn.
source_passage: The action having proceeded for a few minutes, agitation is stopped, and, after allowing to settle, the green liquor is withdrawn.

statement: When palm oil is sufficiently bleached by the bichromate process, the oil is finally washed, without further heating, with hot water (which may contain salt) to remove the last traces of chrome liquor.
source_passage: When sufficiently bleached the oil is finally washed (without further heating) with hot water (which may contain salt), to remove the last traces of chrome liquor.

statement: If the bichromate bleaching of palm oil is carried out carefully, the colouring matter of the oil will be completely oxidised.
source_passage: If the above operation is carried out carefully, the colouring matter will be completely oxidised.

statement: During the bleaching of palm oil the temperature should not be allowed to rise above 130 deg. F. (54 deg. C.), otherwise the resultant oil on saponification is apt to yield a soap of a "foxy" colour.
source_passage: It is important, however, that the temperature should not be allowed to rise above 130 deg. F. (54 deg. C.) during the bleaching of palm oil, otherwise the resultant oil on saponification is apt to yield a soap of a "foxy" colour.

statement: Palm oil bleached by the bichromate process retains the characteristic violet odour of the original oil.
source_passage: The bleached oil retains the characteristic violet odour of the original oil.

statement: Dilute sulphuric acid, or a mixture of dilute sulphuric acid and common salt, has been suggested in place of muriatic acid in the bichromate bleaching of palm oil.
source_passage: It has been suggested to use dilute sulphuric acid, or a mixture of this and common salt, in the place of muriatic acid in the above process.

statement: The deep colouring matter of crude cotton-seed oil, together with the mucilaginous and resinous principles, is removed by refining with caustic soda lye.
source_passage: The deep colouring matter of crude cotton-seed oil, together with the mucilaginous and resinous principles, are removed by refining with caustic soda lye.

statement: The chief aim of the refiner of crude cotton-seed oil is to remove the impurities without saponifying any of the neutral oil.
source_passage: The chief aim of the refiner is to remove these impurities without saponifying any of the neutral oil.

statement: In refining crude cotton-seed oil, the percentage of free fatty acids in the oil determines the quantity of caustic lye required, which must only be sufficient to remove this acidity.
source_passage: The percentage of free fatty acids in the oil will determine the quantity of caustic lye required, which must only be sufficient to remove this acidity.

statement: In refining crude cotton-seed oil, once the free acidity is determined, the quantity of caustic soda lye needed to neutralise it is diluted with water to 12 deg. or 15 deg. Tw. (8 deg. or 10 deg. B.), and the refining is carried out in three stages.
source_passage: Having determined the amount of free acidity, the quantity of caustic soda lye necessary to neutralise it is diluted with water to 12 deg. or 15 deg. Tw. (8 deg. or 10 deg. B.), and the refining process carried out in three stages.

statement: In the first stage of refining crude cotton-seed oil, the oil is heated in a tank by a closed steam coil to 100 deg. F. (38 deg. C.), a third of the weak caustic soda lye is added in a fine stream or by a sprinkler, and the whole is well agitated with a mechanical agitator or by blowing air through a pipe laid on the bottom of the tank.
source_passage: The oil is placed in a suitable tank and heated by means of a closed steam coil to 100 deg. F. (38 deg. C.), a third of the necessary weak caustic soda lye added in a fine stream or by means of a sprinkler, and the whole well agitated with a mechanical agitator or by blowing a current of air through a pipe laid on the bottom of the tank.

statement: Prolonged agitation of cotton-seed oil with air tends to oxidise the oil, which increases its specific gravity and refractive index and produces a reddish soap in the soap-pan.
source_passage: Prolonged agitation with air has a tendency to oxidise the oil, which increases its specific gravity and refractive index, and will be found in the soap-pan to produce a reddish soap.

statement: As the caustic soda refining of cotton-seed oil proceeds, the temperature may be carefully raised by means of the steam coil to 120 deg. F. (49 deg. C.).
source_passage: As the treatment proceeds, the temperature may be carefully raised, by means of the steam coil, to 120 deg. F. (49 deg. C.).

statement: In refining crude cotton-seed oil, after the first treatment has proceeded fifteen minutes the tank contents are allowed to rest, and settling should be prolonged as much as possible, say overnight, so that the impurities precipitate well and carry down the least amount of entangled oil.
source_passage: The first treatment having proceeded fifteen minutes, the contents of the tank are allowed to rest; the settling should be prolonged as much as possible, say overnight, to allow the impurities to precipitate well, and carry down the least amount of entangled oil.

statement: In the second stage of refining crude cotton-seed oil, after the coloured foots are withdrawn, the second portion of weak caustic soda solution is agitated with the partially refined oil, which is then allowed to rest and the settled coloured liquor drawn off.
source_passage: Having withdrawn these coloured "foots," the second portion of the weak caustic soda solution is agitated with the partially refined oil, and, when the latter is sufficiently treated, it is allowed to rest and the settled coloured liquor drawn off as before.

statement: The final stage of refining crude cotton-seed oil is performed in the same manner as the two previous stages, and on settling a clear yellow oil separates.
source_passage: The oil is now ready for the final treatment, which is performed in the same manner as the two previous ones. On settling, a clear yellow oil separates.

statement: Refined cotton-seed oil may, if desired, be brightened and filtered to produce a marketable article, but this may be omitted if the oil is refined for own use in the soap-house.
source_passage: If desired, the oil may be brightened and filtered, after refining to produce a marketable article, but if it is being refined for own use in the soap-house, this may be omitted.

statement: "Mucilage" is the trade name for the residue or "foots" produced during the refining of crude cotton-seed oil.
source_passage: The residue or "foots" produced during the refining of crude cotton-seed oil, known in the trade as "mucilage," may be converted into "soapstock" as mentioned in the preceding chapter, or decomposed by a mineral acid and made into "black grease" ready for distillation by superheated steam.

statement: The foots from refining crude cotton-seed oil may be converted into "soapstock".
source_passage: The residue or "foots" produced during the refining of crude cotton-seed oil, known in the trade as "mucilage," may be converted into "soapstock" as mentioned in the preceding chapter, or decomposed by a mineral acid and made into "black grease" ready for distillation by superheated steam.

statement: The foots from refining crude cotton-seed oil may alternatively be decomposed by a mineral acid and made into "black grease", which is ready for distillation by superheated steam.
source_passage: The residue or "foots" produced during the refining of crude cotton-seed oil, known in the trade as "mucilage," may be converted into "soapstock" as mentioned in the preceding chapter, or decomposed by a mineral acid and made into "black grease" ready for distillation by superheated steam.

statement: Vegetable oils other than palm oil and cotton-seed oil come to the soap-maker's hand in a refined condition.
source_passage: The other vegetable oils come to the soap-maker's hand in a refined condition; occasionally, however, it is desirable to remove a portion of the free fatty acids, which treatment also causes the colouring matter to be preciptated.

statement: Occasionally it is desirable to remove a portion of the free fatty acids from refined vegetable oils, and this treatment also causes the colouring matter to be precipitated.
source_passage: The other vegetable oils come to the soap-maker's hand in a refined condition; occasionally, however, it is desirable to remove a portion of the free fatty acids, which treatment also causes the colouring matter to be preciptated.

statement: Removal of free fatty acids from vegetable oils is effected by bringing the oil and a weak solution of caustic lye into intimate contact.
source_passage: This is effected by bringing the oil and a weak solution of caustic lye into intimate contact.

statement: Cocoa-nut oil is often treated with a weak solution of caustic lye to remove free fatty acids.
source_passage: Cocoa-nut oil is often treated in this manner.

statement: Sometimes the only treatment needed to remove free fatty acids from a vegetable oil is to agitate the oil well with 1-1/2 per cent. of its weight of a 12 deg. Tw. (8 deg. B.) solution of caustic soda and allow it to settle.
source_passage: Sometimes it is only necessary to well agitate the oil with 1-1/2 per cent. of its weight of a 12 deg. Tw. (8 deg. B.) solution of caustic soda and allow to settle.

statement: The foots from the caustic soda treatment of vegetable oils are utilised in the soap-pan.
source_passage: The foots are utilised in the soap-pan.

statement: Tallows are often greatly improved by alkaline treatment with weak caustic lye at 165 deg. F. (73 deg. C.).
source_passage: Tallows are often greatly improved by the above alkaline treatment at 165 deg. F. (73 deg. C.).

statement: Alkaline treatment of tallow is one of the best methods and has advantages over acid processes because the caustic soda removes the free acid and bodies of aldehyde nature, which are most probably the result of oxidation or polymerisation.
source_passage: It is one of the best methods and possesses advantages over acid processes--the caustic soda removes the free acid and bodies of aldehyde nature, which are most probably the result of oxidation or polymerisation, whereas the neutral fat is not attacked, and further, the alkaline foots can be used in the production of soap.

statement: A further advantage of alkaline treatment of tallow over acid processes is that the neutral fat is not attacked by the caustic soda.
source_passage: It is one of the best methods and possesses advantages over acid processes--the caustic soda removes the free acid and bodies of aldehyde nature, which are most probably the result of oxidation or polymerisation, whereas the neutral fat is not attacked, and further, the alkaline foots can be used in the production of soap.

statement: A further advantage of alkaline treatment of tallow over acid processes is that the alkaline foots can be used in the production of soap.
source_passage: It is one of the best methods and possesses advantages over acid processes--the caustic soda removes the free acid and bodies of aldehyde nature, which are most probably the result of oxidation or polymerisation, whereas the neutral fat is not attacked, and further, the alkaline foots can be used in the production of soap.

statement: Bone fat often contains calcium (lime) salts, which are very objectionable substances in a soap-pan.
source_passage: _Bone fat_ often contains calcium (lime) salts, which are very objectionable substances in a soap-pan.

statement: The calcium (lime) salts in bone fat must be removed by treatment with hydrochloric or sulphuric acid.
source_passage: These impurities must be removed by a treatment with hydrochloric or sulphuric acid.

statement: Hydrochloric acid is preferable to sulphuric acid for removing lime salts from bone fat because the lime salt formed is readily soluble and easily removed.
source_passage: The former acid is preferable, as the lime salt formed is readily soluble and easily removed.

statement: In the acid treatment of bone fat, the fat is agitated with a weak solution of acid in a lead-lined tank by blowing in steam.
source_passage: The fat is agitated with a weak solution of acid in a lead-lined tank by blowing in steam, and when the treatment is complete and the waste liquor withdrawn, the last traces of acid are well washed out of the liquid fat with hot water.

statement: In the acid treatment of bone fat, when the treatment is complete and the waste liquor withdrawn, the last traces of acid are well washed out of the liquid fat with hot water.
source_passage: The fat is agitated with a weak solution of acid in a lead-lined tank by blowing in steam, and when the treatment is complete and the waste liquor withdrawn, the last traces of acid are well washed out of the liquid fat with hot water.

statement: Of the several methods suggested for bleaching rosin, some alter the constitution of the rosin, and in others the cost is too great or the process impracticable.
source_passage: Several methods have been suggested for bleaching rosin; in some instances the constitution of the rosin is altered, and in others the cost is too great or the process impracticable.

statement: The aim of rosin bleaching processes must be the elimination of the colouring matter without altering the original properties of the rosin.
source_passage: The aim of these processes must necessarily be the elimination of the colouring matter without altering the original properties of the substance.

statement: Rosin is best bleached by converting it into a resinate of soda by boiling it with a solution of either caustic soda or carbonated alkali.
source_passage: This is best carried out by converting the rosin into a resinate of soda by boiling it with a solution of either caustic soda or carbonated alkali.

statement: In the caustic soda process for bleaching rosin, 37 cwt. of 17 deg. Tw. (11 deg. B.) caustic soda lye is heated, 20 cwt. of rosin broken into pieces is added, boiling continues until all the resinate is homogeneous, then 1-1/2 cwt. of salt is added and the boiling prolonged a little.
source_passage: The process is commenced by heating 37 cwt. of 17 deg. Tw. (11 deg. B.) caustic soda lye, and adding 20 cwt. of rosin, broken into pieces, and continuing the boiling until all the resinate is homogeneous, when an addition of 1-1/2 cwt. of salt is made and the boiling prolonged a little.

statement: In the caustic soda process for bleaching rosin, on resting the coloured liquor rises to the surface of the resinate and may be siphoned off or pumped away through a skimmer pipe, and the resinate is further washed with water containing a little salt.
source_passage: On resting, the coloured liquor rises to the surface of the resinate, and may be siphoned off (or pumped away through a skimmer pipe) and the resinate further washed with water containing a little salt.

statement: The carbonated alkali process for bleaching rosin is performed in a similar manner to the caustic soda process.
source_passage: The treatment with carbonated alkali is performed in a similar manner.

statement: In the carbonated alkali process for bleaching rosin, a solution of 2-3/4 cwt. of soda ash (58 deg.) in about four times its weight of water is heated and 20 cwt. of rosin broken into small pieces is added.
source_passage: A solution, consisting of 2-3/4 cwt. of soda ash (58 deg.), in about four times its weight of water, is heated and 20 cwt. of rosin, broken into small pieces, added.

statement: In the carbonated alkali process for bleaching rosin, the whole is heated by means of the open steam coil, and care must be taken to avoid boiling over.
source_passage: The whole is heated by means of the open steam coil, and care must be taken to avoid boiling over.

statement: In the carbonated alkali process for bleaching rosin, frothing takes place owing to the liberation of CO_{2} gas.
source_passage: Owing to the liberation of CO_{2} gas, frothing takes place.

statement: A large number of patents have been granted for the preparation of resinate of soda, and many methods devised to obviate the boiling over.
source_passage: A large number of patents have been granted for the preparation of resinate of soda, and many methods devised to obviate the boiling over.

statement: One suggested method to obviate boiling over in preparing resinate of soda is mixing the rosin and soda ash (or only a portion of the soda ash) prior to dissolving in water.
source_passage: Some suggest mixing the rosin and soda ash (or only a portion of the soda ash) prior to dissolving in water; others saponify in a boiler connected with a trap which returns the resinate to the pan and allows the carbonic-acid gas to escape or to be collected.

statement: Another suggested method to obviate boiling over in preparing resinate of soda is saponifying in a boiler connected with a trap which returns the resinate to the pan and allows the carbonic-acid gas to escape or to be collected.
source_passage: Some suggest mixing the rosin and soda ash (or only a portion of the soda ash) prior to dissolving in water; others saponify in a boiler connected with a trap which returns the resinate to the pan and allows the carbonic-acid gas to escape or to be collected.

statement: With due precaution, the carbonated alkali method of preparing resinate of soda can be easily worked in open vessels.
source_passage: With due precaution the method can be easily worked in open vessels, and, using the above proportions, there will be sufficient uncombined rosin remaining to allow the resultant product to be pumped into the soap with which it is intended to intermix it, where it will be finally saponified thoroughly.

statement: Using 2-3/4 cwt. of soda ash to 20 cwt. of rosin leaves sufficient uncombined rosin for the resinate product to be pumped into the soap with which it is to be intermixed, where it is finally saponified thoroughly.
source_passage: With due precaution the method can be easily worked in open vessels, and, using the above proportions, there will be sufficient uncombined rosin remaining to allow the resultant product to be pumped into the soap with which it is intended to intermix it, where it will be finally saponified thoroughly.

statement: In the carbonated alkali process for bleaching 20 cwt. of rosin, the salt required, 1-1/2 cwt., may be added to the solution before the rosin or sprinkled in towards the finish of the boiling.
source_passage: The salt required, which, in the example given, would be 1-1/2 cwt., may be added to the solution prior to the addition of rosin or sprinkled in towards the finish of the boiling.

statement: In the carbonated alkali process for bleaching rosin, when the whole has been sufficiently boiled and rested, the liquor containing the colouring matter floats over the resinate and, after removal, may be replaced by another washing.
source_passage: When the whole has been sufficiently boiled and allowed to rest, the liquor containing the colouring matter will float over the resinate, and, after removal, may be replaced by another washing.

statement: Many other methods have been suggested for bleaching, refining and treating materials intended for saponification, but the practical processes described in Chapter IV for palm oil, cotton-seed oil, vegetable oils, animal fats, bone fat and rosin are successfully employed.
source_passage: Many other methods have been suggested for the bleaching, refining and treatment of materials intended for saponification, but the above practical processes are successfully employed.

statement: All fats and oils, after being melted by the aid of steam, must be allowed to settle thoroughly, and the condensed water and impurities withdrawn through a trap arrangement for collecting the fatty matter.
source_passage: All fats and oils after being melted by the aid of steam must be allowed to thoroughly settle, and the condensed water and impurities withdrawn through a trap arrangement for collecting the fatty matter.

statement: Molten, settled fatty materials en route to the soap-pan should be passed through sieves fine enough to free them from suspended matter.
source_passage: The molten settled fatty materials _en route_ to the soap-pan should be passed through sieves sufficiently fine to free them from suspended matter.
